subject: Critical Thinking
title: Ad Hominem: Attacking the Person, Not the Argument
description: A fast breakdown of Ad Hominem: Attacking the Person, Not the Argument for builders.

hook.text: 'You're not a scientist, so your climate data doesn't count.' The data is either valid or it'sn't, regardless of who.

buildup.text: Ad hominem: attacking the person making the argument instead of addressing the argument itself.

discovery.text: It comes in flavors: abusive (you're stupid), circumstantial (you're biased), and tu quoque (you do it too).

twist.text: Sometimes character IS relevant – a pathological liar's testimony matters less.

climax.text: Ad hominem is the most common fallacy in political debate.

punchline.text: Attack the argument, not the arguer. Or admit you can't.

quiz.question: When is ad hominem a fallacy?
options: When character attacks replace engagement with the actual argument

details.summary: Ad hominem attacks the person making an argument rather than the argument itself. A speaker's character, motives, or background are irrelevant to whether their reasoning is valid.
details.whyItMatters: Ad hominem is the most common debate tactic on social media and in politics. Recognizing it prevents you from dismissing valid arguments because of who presents them.
takeaways: Attack arguments, not the people who make them
A speaker's flaws do not invalidate their reasoning
Questioning motives is legitimate only when credibility itself is the issue

faq.question: Is pointing out someone's conflict of interest an ad hominem fallacy?
faq.answer: Not always. When credibility is directly relevant (such as a paid spokesperson), questioning motives is legitimate. It becomes ad hominem when the personal attack replaces engagement with the actual argument.

faq.question: Why is ad hominem so common in political discourse?
faq.answer: Attacking a person is easier and more emotionally satisfying than dismantling their argument. It also works on audiences who use the speaker's likability as a proxy for the truth of their claims.
